<details>
  <summary><b>Daily Journal</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/jianzhangg/opencode-daily-journal" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Auto-journal every conversation into daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md, record-only (never injects)</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    An OpenCode V2 plugin that keeps a daily journal of your conversations. When a session turn finishes, the exchange is summarized into a diary entry and appended to daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md. Record only, never inject: entries are plain Markdown on disk and are never added to session context unless you explicitly ask the agent to read them. Writes are concurrency-safe (file lock + append-only + idempotent markers, so simultaneous sessions never overwrite or duplicate each other), and summaries use a model fallback chain (session model, then other configured models, then a raw excerpt) so nothing is lost when a model is unavailable.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/jianzhangg/opencode-daily-journal">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

<details>
  <summary><b>deja</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/vshulcz/deja-vu" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Recall what you already did in your other coding agents</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    opencode remembers its own sessions. deja answers the other question: what you did in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Zed and fifteen more agents on this machine — including the months before you installed anything.

A local Go binary indexes the transcripts those agents already wrote to disk, and the plugin gives the model six tools over that index: recall past sessions by error or symbol, read the digest of one session, see which sessions discussed a file before you edit it, ask what this machine actually ran after a given error, and store a decision worth keeping. Recall also arrives unasked — once per session on the system prompt, and a relevance pass per prompt that stays silent when history has no answer.

BM25 over local files. No LLM, no embeddings, no network. Credentials are redacted at index time.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/vshulcz/deja-vu">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a> &nbsp;•&nbsp; <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-deja">📦 <b>npm</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

  <blockquote>
    Claude Code's autocompact, with a knob. Compacts a session before the model's real context limit, at a token count you choose per session. <details>
  <summary><b>OpenCode Crosstalk</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/MrDoe/opencode-crosstalk" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Peer discovery, messaging, and expiring file leases between concurrent OpenCode sessions</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    Coordination for agents that share a workspace. Six tools let concurrent sessions
discover each other, talk to each other, and take exclusive expiring leases on the
files they are editing, so two agents never rewrite the same file at once.

- `crosstalk_status` / `crosstalk_peers` — declare a role, goal, and working set, then list who is running, what they declared, and what they hold
- `crosstalk_send` / `crosstalk_inbox` — message a session, a role, or everyone; mail lands in the recipient's mailbox and is injected into its current turn when the session is live
- `crosstalk_claim` — atomic lease on files or named resources; a refusal names the holder and when the lease expires
- `crosstalk_wait` — block until a peer goes idle or a resource is released, instead of sleeping and re-checking

Identity comes from the session rather than from tool input, so no session can
release another's lease or read another's mail. All six tools share one permission
action (`crosstalk`), so a project can allow or deny coordination with a single
rule. The core coordination logic (presence registry, mailboxes, claim table) is
host-free and unit tested — the plugin imports nothing from OpenCode outside its
single entry point.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/MrDoe/opencode-crosstalk">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

  <blockquote>
    Laya Drift monitors whether an OpenCode agent is staying aligned with its original plan over long-running sessions. It uses the Laya decision model to embed session state, compares the current semantic state against a calibrated baseline with Jensen-Shannon divergence, and surfaces a live drift score in the OpenCode UI. When drift gets high, it can inject the score into the system prompt so the agent can self-correct. Sessions can also be recalibrated to establish a new baseline after an intentional change in direction.

<h4>Security & Sandboxing <sub>(13)</sub></h4>

<details>
  <summary><b>Aegis-DevOps</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/moneytool/aegis-devops" height="14"/> <code>V1 only</code> - <i>Blocks kubectl delete, terraform destroy or DROP TABLE unless your signed policy allows it</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    A tool.execute.before plugin that checks every bash command OpenCode wants to run (kubectl, terraform/tofu, aws/az/gcloud, helm, argocd, git, SQL) against a signed, authority-checked policy before it runs. A rule only counts if it hasn't been edited since it was signed and its author was allowed to write that kind of rule, so a line planted in a ticket can't become policy. Only active in projects with a .aegis/ policy. Install with `pip install aegis-devops &amp;&amp; aegis install opencode`.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/moneytool/aegis-devops">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>

  <blockquote>
    Aftermath is a post-failure recovery skill for OpenCode. When something breaks — a test suite goes green to red, the same error recurs, a destructive command looms, or the user says &quot;you broke it&quot; — it stops forward motion, reverts the actual bad hunk instead of patching around it, and returns the session to last-known-good. Includes four intensity levels (lite/full/ultra/off), four slash commands (status, revert, audit, log), and lifecycle tripwires for test failures, repeat errors, and destructive commands.

<details>
  <summary><b>Stay Awake</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/AuroraAeon/opencode-stay-awake" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Keep the computer awake only while a session is generating</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    Long agent runs (model streaming, tool execution, compaction, rate-limit retries) routinely take minutes with no user input, and default OS power settings treat that as idle and suspend mid-prompt. This plugin holds a system sleep inhibitor for exactly as long as any session is generating, then releases it — caffeinate -dims -w &lt;server pid&gt; on macOS, systemd-inhibit on Linux, no-op elsewhere. Busy detection is event-driven rather than polling, so a tool call that runs for minutes keeps its work item open instead of being released mid-run. Every inhibitor is bound to the server pid and a stale cap bounds any lost end event, so the machine can never be wedged awake. Zero dependencies, MIT.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/AuroraAeon/opencode-stay-awake">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

<h4>Code Intelligence <sub>(4)</sub></h4>

<details>
  <summary><b>Morph Fast Apply</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/JRedeker/opencode-morph-fast-apply" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>10,500+ tokens/sec code editing</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    Integrates Morph's Fast Apply API for faster code editing with lazy edit markers and unified diff output.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/JRedeker/opencode-morph-fast-apply">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

<details>
  <summary><b>OpenCode Indexing</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/Javierkaiser/opencode-indexing" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Semantic code search for OpenCode that reuses Kilo Code's index and keeps its own incremental one.</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    Adds semantic (vector) code search to OpenCode. It reads Kilo Code's existing
index (Qdrant ws-* collections and Kilo's local LanceDB) without ever modifying
it, and can import those vectors and chunks at zero embedding cost, then keep
its own incremental index (Qdrant oc-* collections or embedded LanceDB) keyed
on a per-file SHA-256. Search merges results from both indexes, so semantic
search keeps working even when Kilo is not installed, is disabled, or its index
is stale.

- Reuse Kilo Code's index read-only, importing vectors without re-embedding
- Own incremental index with manifest-based freshness (new/changed/deleted only)
- Vector-store agnostic: Qdrant or embedded LanceDB
- Settings and index actions from the TUI, Desktop and web clients
- Supported embedding providers: Mistral, OpenAI, Ollama, Gemini, Voyage,
  OpenRouter and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/Javierkaiser/opencode-indexing">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a> &nbsp;•&nbsp; <a href="https://github.com/Javierkaiser/opencode-indexing#readme">📖 <b>Docs</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

<details>
  <summary><b>OpenCodeRAG</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/MrDoe/OpenCodeRAG" height="14"/> <code>V2</code> - <i>Local-first RAG plugin for semantic code search with tree-sitter chunking and LanceDB</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    A local-first Retrieval-Augmented Generation plugin for OpenCode that enables semantic code
search across your workspace. Features AST-aware chunking via tree-sitter (19 languages),
incremental indexing with file-change detection, watch mode for live re-indexing, and
configurable embeddings via Ollama (default) or OpenAI. Includes a CLI (index, query, status,
clear) and an OpenCode plugin with a chunk retrieval tool + automatic chat.message file
suggestions. All processing stays local by default — no data leaves the machine.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/MrDoe/OpenCodeRAG">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

(PLAN → DO → CHECK → ACT) with transition gates, evidence-based verification,
escalation accounting, durable status, and recovery after compaction.

- **pdca** — domain-neutral cycle; the task's PLAN selects the means and the verification method.
- **pdca-coder** — stack-agnostic executor for software tasks (code, tests, docs, refactoring, config).
- **pdca-dotnet** — the same cycle tuned for .NET/C# repositories.
- **pdca-collection** — a batch of tasks run as parallel PDCA lanes (worktree per group, `--no-ff` merge of completed groups).

Roles (planner, coder, check, scout, escalate) are bound by the host, so the
skills stay model- and provider-neutral.

<details>
  <summary><b>cowork-to-code-bridge</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/abhinaykrupa/cowork-to-code-bridge" height="14"/> - <i>Run agent tasks on your own machine from a sandboxed caller, with no inbound port</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    A local-first async bridge that lets an agent running somewhere else — a cloud sandbox, a container, a hosted chat session, a CI job — execute work on the developer's real machine. There is no network listener, no inbound port and no tunnel: a daemon watches a shared directory, the remote side drops a JSON task file in, and the daemon runs it locally and writes a result file back. Any shared folder works (bind mount, Syncthing, Dropbox, NFS). Execution is allow-listed — only scripts installed into the daemon's scripts directory can run, so a remote caller cannot request arbitrary shell. Tasks are non-blocking and cancellable (SIGTERM to the whole process group, then SIGKILL after a grace period), output is size-capped while streaming with truncation reported, and results carry real exit codes. Ships ~25 scripts (host health, disk, ports, docker ps/logs, git status, package updates), a wrapper that hands a whole task to a local CLI coding agent, and an MCP proxy that relays JSON-RPC to local stdio MCP servers. Python client, stdlib-only, MIT, macOS and Linux.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/abhinaykrupa/cowork-to-code-bridge">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

  <blockquote>
    Records an OpenCode session without modifying it, then replays that run with the network off and reproduces it with the network off, or forks it from any step so the model is the only thing that changed. Because OpenCode keeps its provider origin in opencode.json rather than an environment variable, there is nothing to redirect: the adapter terminates the TLS OpenCode opened itself using a per-run CA that only the launched process trusts and that is deleted when the run ends, and your config is left untouched. Alongside the model traffic it records shell exit codes and timing, per-turn file changes and MCP calls, all on one timeline. Apache-2.0, Node 20+, and the trace format is a published spec so other readers can be written against it.
    <br><br>

Each round is classified from trajectory state — round position, tool calls and their results, failure evidence, context pressure — and a deterministic policy maps class to tier (failure → strong, exploration → cheap, first-turn → mid). An optional semantic judge (TypeSafe Jev) runs only on rounds the policy cannot classify, and is fail-open. The harness loop is untouched.
Exposes an OpenAI-compatible local proxy at 127.0.0.1:8787/v1. From OpenCode, `npm run connect:opencode` writes only a provider.sabi entry and the adaptive alias is `sabi/sabi-code`; fixed baselines `sabi/sabi-cheap`, `sabi/sabi-mid` and `sabi/sabi-strong` are available for comparison. Borrowed-auth passthrough is supported: the harness keeps its own credential and Sabi rewrites only model. Decisions and cost are inspectable via `npm run report`.

Works with OpenCode via MCP (hosted https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp with OAuth, or local `squirrel mcp` over stdio) to run audits, read reports and fix findings, or via the agent-skills format with `npx skills add squirrelscan/squirrelscan`. Free local audits, GitHub Action, MIT CLI and rules.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/squirrelscan/squirrelscan">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a> &nbsp;•&nbsp; <a href="https://squirrelscan.com">📖 <b>Docs</b></a>

<details>
  <summary><b>staffetta</b> <img src="https://badgen.net/github/stars/RaffaeleSpezia/staffetta" height="14"/> - <i>Model-decided context handoff: close a milestone, write memory to disk, restart with a clean session</i></summary>
  <blockquote>
    A relay-race alternative to compaction for long-running agents. Instead of a threshold rewriting the conversation in place, the agent itself decides when a milestone is closed, writes what the next session needs to disk, and hands over — the session ends and a fresh one picks up the baton. Memory lives in files (MEMORY.md overwritten, JOURNAL.md append-only, AGENTS.md for rules), so it is readable, diffable, correctable and survives the session. Four tools the agent calls itself: checkpoint (verifies by checksum that memory actually changed, rejects journal entries with no numbers in them, detects tampering with older entries), ask (pauses for a human decision, requires the agent to state what it would do without an answer), resume (refuses until the decision is written down), and loop (reopens the session and nothing else — it ends when the model declares --done or --blocked, not when a counter infers it). Measured on a local KAT-Coder V2.5 via llama.cpp: 7 milestones closed autonomously, 7 of 7 checkpoints invoked unprompted, 587 tests green, ~5,500 tokens of context per round instead of a compacted session restarting from 142,000 — and it does not grow across rounds. Pure bash, no dependencies; adapters/opencode/loop.sh is the opencode adapter and everything under core/ works with any agent that can run a shell command.
    <br><br>
    <a href="https://github.com/RaffaeleSpezia/staffetta">🔗 <b>View Repository</b></a>
  </blockquote>
</details>

Implementation is dispatched to parallel test-driven subagents; a review panel with distinct lenses (quality, spec and guardrail compliance, cross-module integration) then returns a severity-graded verdict and drives a bounded fix loop until the code is approved. Root-cause analysis is evidence-based rather than a guess: competing hypotheses are falsified against logs, traces, metrics, code and git history before any fix is written. Capability specs follow the OpenSpec directory convention, so a repository initialized by the OpenSpec CLI works as-is. Nothing is written into your project - the guardrails are read in place at runtime, and there is no CLI or state machine to install.
